s0003.literal: Xiao Ji; Lu Qiong; his son Congdian; Gu Ye; Fu Zhi; Zhang Hua
s0003.idiomatic: Xiao Ji; Lu Qiong; his son Congdian; Gu Ye; Fu Zhi; Zhang Hua

s0004.literal: Xiao Ji, styled Xiaokang, was a native of Lanling in Donghai.
s0004.idiomatic: Xiao Ji, styled Xiaokang, came from Lanling in Donghai commandery.

s0005.literal: From youth he loved learning and was broadly versed in the classics and histories; he submitted more than thirty items of doubt in the Zuo Commentary to Liang's Emperor Wu, and the Masters of Writing for the People Zhang Zuan of Fanyang and the Minister of Ceremonies Liu Zhiliao of Nanyang both discussed them with Ji—Zuan and the others could not stand against him.
s0005.idiomatic: From boyhood he loved books and mastered the classics and histories. He put more than thirty questions on the Zuo Commentary before Liang's Emperor Wu; Zhang Zuan of Fanyang, vice director of the masters of writing, and Liu Zhiliao of Nanyang, minister of ceremonies, debated them with him—and could not hold their ground.

s0006.literal: On leaving the purple he was made Secretariat Gentleman of Liang and promoted to groom of the heir apparent.
s0006.idiomatic: He entered service as a Liang secretariat gentleman, then became groom of the heir apparent.

s0007.literal: He took part in pacifying Hou Jing and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Songyang, fief five hundred households.
s0007.idiomatic: He shared in the campaign that crushed Hou Jing and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Songyang, with a fief of five hundred households.

s0008.literal: When the Founder held the frontier post at Xuzhou, he made Ji Bright Prestige General and chief secretary on the northern campaign staff.
s0008.idiomatic: When the Founder was holding Xuzhou as his command, he made Ji bright-prestige general and chief secretary on the northern campaign staff.

s0009.literal: In the second year of Chengsheng he was summoned as Secretariat Vice Director and moved to regular attendant of the communicating scattered cavalry.
s0009.idiomatic: In Chengsheng year 2 (553) he was summoned as secretariat vice director, then made regular attendant of the communicating scattered cavalry.

s0010.literal: When Emperor Wen was interior administrator of Kuaiji, he again made Ji chief secretary of the Firm Resolution establishment and promoted him to left chief secretary of the Secretariat.
s0010.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen governed Kuaiji, he again made Ji chief secretary of the firm-resolution establishment and soon promoted him to left chief secretary of the secretariat.

s0011.literal: When Emperor Wen took the throne, Ji was made palace attendant.
s0011.idiomatic: When Emperor Wen succeeded, Ji was made palace attendant.

s0012.literal: Soon he was moved to grand steward of the imperial household; he mourned his birth mother and did not accept the post.
s0012.idiomatic: Soon he was named grand steward of the imperial household, but mourning his birth mother he declined the appointment.

s0013.literal: Ji assisted two rulers and received favor of exceptional depth; rewards and gifts exceeded the common run.
s0013.idiomatic: Ji served two sovereigns with uncommon trust; rewards and gifts outstripped the usual measure.

s0014.literal: In succession he held Lanling, Yangxian, Linjin, and Lin'an—wherever he went his reputation and achievement stood out.
s0014.idiomatic: He governed in turn Lanling, Yangxian, Linjin, and Lin'an, and everywhere left a name for solid achievement.

s0015.literal: At the beginning of Taijian he entered court as Minister of the Five Armies; together with Left Vice Director Xu Ling, Special Emeritus Zhou Hongzheng, Minister of Revenue Wang Chang, Editorial footnote marker 1. Scattered-Cavalry Regular Attendant Yuan Xian, he all attended the eastern palace.
s0015.idiomatic: At the start of Taijian (569) he entered court as minister of the five armies, and with left vice director Xu Ling, special emeritus Zhou Hongzheng, minister of revenue Wang Chang, [1] and scattered-cavalry regular attendant Yuan Xian he attended the eastern palace together.

s0016.literal: He again became chief secretary of the Secretariat.
s0016.idiomatic: He again became chief secretary of the secretariat.

s0017.literal: Soon he was given Minister of Revenue and additionally led the Feathered Forest guard.
s0017.idiomatic: Soon he was made minister of revenue and also led the feathered forest guard.

s0018.literal: He was moved to libationer of the National University, still leading the Feathered Forest as before.
s0018.idiomatic: He was moved to libationer of the national university while still leading the feathered forest.

s0019.literal: He was given the additional posts of Grand Master with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon and concurrently Defender of the Secure Virtue Palace.
s0019.idiomatic: He was further made grand master with golden seal and purple ribbon and concurrently defender of the secure virtue palace.

s0020.literal: Soon he was moved to Benevolent Prestige General and chief secretary of Yangzhou.
s0020.idiomatic: Soon he was made benevolent-prestige general and chief secretary of Yangzhou.

s0021.literal: Emperor Xuan once ordered the Yangzhou bureau records taken for his own inspection; seeing Ji's entries orderly and thorough, the documents without obstruction or harm, he turned to those beside him and said, "I had expected Chief Secretary Xiao to excel in the classics—who would have said he was this skilled at intricate administration as well?"
s0021.idiomatic: Emperor Xuan once ordered the Yangzhou bureau papers brought for his own reading. Ji had arranged everything with meticulous clarity, the documents flowing without snag or tangle. The emperor turned to his attendants and said, "I expected Chief Secretary Xiao to shine in the classics—not that he would master tangled administration to this degree."

s0022.literal: He was moved to Minister of Ceremonies, given the additional post of Supervising Censor, and again made Grand Master with Golden Seal and Purple Ribbon.
s0022.idiomatic: He was made minister of ceremonies, given the additional post of supervising censor, and again made grand master with golden seal and purple ribbon.

s0023.literal: Before he could take up the appointment he died, aged sixty-six.
s0023.idiomatic: Before he could take office he died, at sixty-six.

s0024.literal: An edict posthumously granted his last office and supplied funeral expenses from the government.
s0024.idiomatic: An edict granted his last office posthumously and supplied his funeral from the treasury.

s0025.literal: Lu Qiong, styled Boyu, was a native of Wu in Wu commandery.
s0025.idiomatic: Lu Qiong, styled Boyu, came from Wu in Wu commandery.

s0026.literal: His grandfather Wan was Liang's chief clerk in the two commanderies of Langye and Pengcheng.
s0026.idiomatic: His grandfather Wan was Liang's chief clerk in Langye and Pengcheng commanderies.

s0027.literal: His father Yungong was Liang's Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate and director of composition.
s0027.idiomatic: His father Yungong was Liang's attendant gentleman of the yellow gate and director of composition.

s0028.literal: Qiong in childhood was clever and thoughtful; at six he composed pentasyllabic verse with considerable literary grace.
s0028.idiomatic: Qiong as a child was quick and thoughtful. At six he wrote pentasyllabic verse with real polish.

s0029.literal: At the end of Datong, Yungong received Liang's Emperor Wu's order to collate weiqi rankings; Dao Gai, Zhu Yi, and others below all gathered—Qiong was then eight sui and before the guests replayed a game from memory, whereupon the capital styled him a divine child.
s0029.idiomatic: Near the end of Datong, Yungong received Emperor Wu of Liang's order to fix the grades of weiqi players. Dao Gai, Zhu Yi, and the rest assembled; Qiong was eight and, before the guests, reconstructed a game from memory. The capital thereafter called him a prodigy.

s0030.literal: Yi spoke of him to the Emperor; an edict summoned him for audience. Qiong's bearing was alert and bright, his advance and retreat measured and careful—the Emperor marveled greatly.
s0030.idiomatic: Zhu Yi spoke of him to the throne, and an edict called him in. Qiong's presence was keen and luminous; he moved with careful grace. The emperor was deeply struck.

s0031.literal: At eleven he mourned his father; his wasting grief showed utmost filial nature. His father's cousin Xiang sighed and said, "This boy will surely bear up the house—what people call 'one is not too few.'"
s0031.idiomatic: At eleven he mourned his father, wasting away with a grief that showed his deepest nature. His father's cousin Xiang sighed and said, "This boy will carry the clan. As they say, one such son is not too few."

s0032.literal: When Hou Jing rebelled, he took his mother to refuge in the western township of the county, toiled at reading day and night without slack, and thereby became broadly learned and skilled at literary composition.
s0032.idiomatic: When Hou Jing rose in rebellion, Qiong took his mother to refuge in the county's western hamlets and read without rest by day or lamp by night, until he was broadly learned and sure with the brush.

s0033.literal: When Emperor Xuan was Secretariat Director he finely sifted his staff; the Minister of Personnel Xu Ling recommended Qiong to Emperor Xuan, saying: "Xin'an Prince's literary officer Lu Qiong has discerning insight, fine and quick; his literature and history suffice for use—he has served in the secretariat long, the left western aide post is vacant and he fits this selection; his rank order is slightly exceeded, but his frustration has built up.
s0033.idiomatic: When Emperor Xuan was secretariat director he chose his staff with care. Minister of personnel Xu Ling recommended Qiong to him, saying, "Lu Qiong, literary officer to the Prince of Xin'an, is sharp in judgment and quick in mind; his command of letters and history is ample. He has lingered in the secretariat too long. The left western aide post stands open and he should fill it—only his rank is a little low, and the delay has pressed on him too long.

s0034.literal: " He was then made left western aide of the Secretariat.
s0034.idiomatic: " He was then made left western aide of the secretariat.

s0035.literal: Soon he additionally held Regular Attendant of the Communicating Scattered Cavalry and went on embassy to Qi.
s0035.idiomatic: Soon he also held regular attendant of the communicating scattered cavalry and went on embassy to Qi.

s0036.literal: In the first year of Taijian he again held his former office and directed records of the eastern palace.
s0036.idiomatic: In Taijian year 1 (569) he again held his former post and directed the eastern palace records.

s0037.literal: He was made junior mentor of the heir apparent and additionally Communicating Affairs Attendant.
s0037.idiomatic: He was made junior mentor of the heir apparent and also communicating affairs attendant.

s0038.literal: He was moved to Secretariat Vice Director and steward of the heir apparent's household.
s0038.idiomatic: He was moved to secretariat vice director and steward of the heir apparent's household.

s0039.literal: The Prince of Changsha was inspector of Jiangzhou and did not follow law and measure; because the prince was young, Emperor Xuan gave Qiong the post of chief secretary to conduct the Jiangzhou establishment and state affairs of the commandery, and concurrently made him interior administrator of Xunyang.
s0039.idiomatic: The Prince of Changsha, as inspector of Jiangzhou, ignored law and precedent. Emperor Xuan, judging him young, made Qiong his chief secretary to run the Jiangzhou establishment and the commandery's state affairs, and concurrently interior administrator of Xunyang.

s0040.literal: Qiong because his mother was old did not wish to go far; the heir apparent also firmly asked to keep him—so in the end he did not go.
s0040.idiomatic: Qiong's mother was old and he did not wish to travel far; the heir apparent also pressed to keep him—and so he never went.

s0041.literal: In succession he was moved to Attendant Gentleman of the Yellow Gate and led the Feathered Forest guard.
s0041.idiomatic: He rose in turn to attendant gentleman of the yellow gate and leader of the feathered forest guard.

s0042.literal: He was moved to junior mentor in the heir apparent's household and led the Footsoldiers Commandant.
s0042.idiomatic: He was made junior mentor in the heir apparent's household and also led the footsoldiers commandant.

s0043.literal: He additionally led the Grand Composition office and compiled the national history.
s0043.idiomatic: He also led the grand composition office and compiled the national history.

s0044.literal: When Houzhu took the throne, Qiong served directly in the Secretariat and directed edicts and proclamations.
s0044.idiomatic: When Houzhu succeeded, Qiong served in the secretariat itself and directed edicts and proclamations.

s0045.literal: Soon he was given Scattered-Cavalry Regular Attendant, additionally Minister of Revenue, and led the grand rectifier of Yangzhou.
s0045.idiomatic: Soon he was made scattered-cavalry regular attendant, additionally minister of revenue, and grand rectifier of Yangzhou.

s0046.literal: In the first year of Zhide he was made Minister of Revenue, took part in directing edicts and proclamations, and jointly decided cases in the Court of Review and the two prisons of Jiankang.
s0046.idiomatic: In Zhide year 1 (583) he was made minister of revenue, shared in directing edicts and proclamations, and jointly judged cases in the court of review and the two Jiankang prisons.

s0047.literal: Earlier Qiong's father Yungong had received Liang's Emperor Wu's order to compile the Record of Auspicious Omens; Qiong set forth its intent and continued it, from Yongding down to Zhide, and brought it to completion as a work in one tradition.
s0047.idiomatic: Earlier his father Yungong, on Liang Emperor Wu's order, had begun the Record of Auspicious Omens. Qiong took up his aim and carried it on from Yongding through Zhide until it stood complete as a single tradition.

s0048.literal: He was moved to Minister of Personnel, his direction of composition unchanged.
s0048.idiomatic: He was moved to minister of personnel while still directing composition.

s0049.literal: Qiong was thorough in genealogies and registers and refined in judging human worth. Earlier, when Minister of Personnel Zong Yuanrao died, Right Vice Director Yuan Xian had recommended Qiong, but Emperor Xuan had not yet used him; now that he held the post, he was called fully equal to the charge, and Houzhu relied on him deeply.
s0049.idiomatic: Qiong knew genealogies and registers down to the last line and judged men with a quiet eye. When Minister of Personnel Zong Yuanrao died, right vice director Yuan Xian had recommended him, but Emperor Xuan had not yet appointed him. Now that he held the office, men said he filled it; Houzhu entrusted him without reserve.

s0050.literal: Qiong's nature was modest and frugal; he did not aggrandize himself. Though rank and expectation rose day by day, his resolve grew only more humble.
s0050.idiomatic: Qiong was modest and frugal and never built himself up. Though rank and renown climbed, his resolve sank lower still.

s0051.literal: Garden, pond, house, and hall—he altered none of them; carriage, horse, and dress—he did not pursue fresh splendor; the seasonal salary of each season he gave away to his clan, and his house held no surplus wealth.
s0051.idiomatic: He changed neither garden nor hall; his carriages and robes never chased new brilliance; each season's stipend he scattered among his kin, and no coin remained at home.

s0052.literal: In his later years he deeply felt that enough was enough and wished to avoid the powerful; he constantly pleaded illness and did not attend to affairs.
s0052.idiomatic: In his later years he felt he had enough and sought to step back from power; again and again he pleaded illness and would not govern.

s0053.literal: Soon he mourned his mother and left office.
s0053.idiomatic: Soon he mourned his mother and left office.

s0054.literal: Earlier, when Qiong attended the eastern palace, his mother followed him in the official quarters; Houzhu rewarded them generously.
s0054.idiomatic: When Qiong had served the eastern palace, his mother lived with him in the official quarters, and Houzhu had rewarded them generously.

s0055.literal: When the coffin returned to his home district, an edict added funeral gifts and also sent the Herald Huang Changgui with a patent to offer libation and sacrifice; Houzhu himself composed the epitaph inscription, and court and countryside alike honored him.
s0055.idiomatic: When the coffin went home, an edict added funeral gifts and sent herald Huang Changgui with a patent to offer libation and sacrifice. Houzhu himself wrote the epitaph, and court and countryside alike took it as honor.

s0056.literal: Qiong's grief for his mother exceeded measure; in the fourth year of Zhide he died, aged fifty.
s0056.idiomatic: Qiong's grief for his mother passed all bounds. In Zhide year 4 (586) he died, at fifty.

s0057.literal: An edict posthumously made him General of the Palace Guard and supplied funeral expenses from the government.
s0057.idiomatic: An edict posthumously made him general of the palace guard and supplied his funeral from the treasury.

s0058.literal: A collection in twenty juan circulated in his day.
s0058.idiomatic: A collection in twenty juan circulated in his time.

s0059.literal: His eldest son Congyi reached the post of literary officer to the Prince of Wuchang.
s0059.idiomatic: His eldest son Congyi rose to literary officer to the Prince of Wuchang.

s0060.literal: His third son Congdian, styled Youyi.
s0060.idiomatic: His third son Congdian, styled Youyi.

s0061.literal: From childhood he was clever and keen.
s0061.idiomatic: From childhood he was clever and keen.

s0062.literal: At eight he read Shen Yue's collected works; seeing a palindrome study inscription, Congdian took up the brush and imitated it, and at once achieved fine effect.
s0062.idiomatic: At eight he read Shen Yue's collected works. Seeing a palindrome study inscription, Congdian took up the brush to match it and at once produced something fine.

s0063.literal: At thirteen he composed a Rhapsody on the Willow; its wording was very beautiful.
s0063.idiomatic: At thirteen he wrote a Rhapsody on the Willow, and its language was very fine.

s0064.literal: At that time Qiong was director of the eastern palace records; the palace staff were all outstanding men of the age—Qiong showed them this rhapsody, and all marveled at his unusual talent.
s0064.idiomatic: Qiong was then directing the eastern palace records; the palace staff were all men of mark in their day. He showed them the rhapsody, and each wondered at the boy's gift.

s0065.literal: His father's cousin Yu especially cherished and loved him; when Yu was near death he entrusted the household's grave registers and books all to Congdian. Congdian thereupon collected Yu's writings into ten juan and also composed a preface to the collection—the writing was very accomplished.
s0065.idiomatic: His father's cousin Yu cherished him above the rest. When Yu was dying he entrusted the household's grave registers and books to Congdian, who gathered Yu's writings into ten juan and wrote a preface—the prose was accomplished throughout.

s0066.literal: Congdian deeply loved learning and was broadly versed in many books; in the History of the Former Han he took special interest.
s0066.idiomatic: Congdian loved learning deeply and ranged through many books; the History of the Former Han was his particular passion.

s0067.literal: At fifteen his home province nominated him as a cultivated talent.
s0067.idiomatic: At fifteen his home province nominated him as cultivated talent.

s0068.literal: On leaving the purple he was made composition aide and moved to groom of the heir apparent.
s0068.idiomatic: He entered service as composition aide, then became groom of the heir apparent.

s0069.literal: At that time Houzhu bestowed verse on Vice Director Jiang Zong and his father Qiong together; Zong ordered Congdian to compose the letter of thanks—in a moment it was done, the writing elegant and the reasoning clear, and Zong marveled greatly.
s0069.idiomatic: Houzhu then bestowed verse on vice director Jiang Zong and on his father Qiong together. Zong had Congdian draft the letter of thanks; in a moment it stood finished, elegant in word and clear in reason, and Zong was astonished.

s0070.literal: Soon he was made literary officer to the Prince of Xinyi and moved to groom who washes the heir apparent's horses.
s0070.idiomatic: Soon he was made literary officer to the Prince of Xinyi, then groom who washes the heir apparent's horses.

s0071.literal: He was again moved to left western aide of the Secretariat and additionally academician of the eastern palace.
s0071.idiomatic: He was again made left western aide of the secretariat and additionally academician of the eastern palace.

s0072.literal: He mourned his father and left office.
s0072.idiomatic: He mourned his father and left office.

s0073.literal: Soon he was summoned as academician of the Virtue Teaching establishment; he firmly declined and did not accept—Houzhu ordered one post kept vacant, awaiting Congdian.
s0073.idiomatic: Soon he was summoned as academician of the virtue-teaching establishment; he firmly declined. Houzhu ordered one post kept vacant, waiting for Congdian.

s0074.literal: Soon Jinling fell; following precedent he was moved to the region west of the passes.
s0074.idiomatic: Soon Jinling fell; by precedent he was moved west of the passes.

s0075.literal: Under Sui he served as Attendant Gentleman and additionally academician of the eastern palace.
s0075.idiomatic: Under Sui he served as attendant gentleman and additionally academician of the eastern palace.

s0076.literal: He was again made composition aide.
s0076.idiomatic: He was again made composition aide.

s0077.literal: Right Vice Director Yang Su memorialized that Congdian should continue Sima Qian's Records of the Historian down to Sui—the book was not completed.
s0077.idiomatic: Right vice director Yang Su memorialized that Congdian should continue Sima Qian's Records of the Historian down to Sui; the book was never finished.

s0078.literal: When the turmoil at the end of Sui came, he lodged in Nanyang commandery and died of illness, aged fifty-seven.
s0078.idiomatic: In the chaos at the end of Sui he lodged in Nanyang commandery and died of illness, at fifty-seven.

s0079.literal: Gu Ye, styled Xifeng, was a native of Wu in Wu commandery.
s0079.idiomatic: Gu Ye, styled Xifeng, came from Wu in Wu commandery.

s0080.literal: His grandfather Ziqiao was a staff officer in the Eastern Central Army Prince of Wuling's establishment.
s0080.idiomatic: His grandfather Ziqiao was a staff officer in the eastern central army establishment of the Prince of Wuling.

s0081.literal: His father Xuan was recorder for the Trustworthy Prestige Prince of Linhe and concurrently the five offices chief clerk of his home commandery; he was known for Confucian learning.
s0081.idiomatic: His father Xuan was recorder for the trustworthy-prestige Prince of Linhe and concurrently five-offices chief clerk of his home commandery, known for Confucian learning.

s0083.literal: At seven he read the Five Classics and grasped their main purport.
s0083.idiomatic: At seven he read the Five Classics and grasped their main purport.

s0084.literal: At nine he could compose prose; he once wrote a Rhapsody on the Sun, and the Area Commander Zhu Yi, on seeing it, marveled.
s0084.idiomatic: At nine he could write prose. He once composed a Rhapsody on the Sun; area commander Zhu Yi read it and marveled.

s0085.literal: At twelve he followed his father to Jian'an and composed two chapters of a Topography of Jian'an.
s0085.idiomatic: At twelve he followed his father to Jian'an and wrote two chapters of a Topography of Jian'an.

s0086.literal: When grown he surveyed the classics and histories in full, with keen memory and silent retention; astronomy and geography, milfoil and tortoise divination, insect scripts and strange characters—there was nothing he did not penetrate.
s0086.idiomatic: Grown, he ranged through the classics and histories with a memory that held without effort; astronomy and geography, milfoil and tortoise divination, insect scripts and strange characters—nothing lay outside his reach.

s0087.literal: In the fourth year of Datong of Liang he was made Erudite of the National University.
s0087.idiomatic: In Liang Datong year 4 (538) he was made erudite of the national university.

s0088.literal: He was moved to recorder in the staff of the Central Army Prince of Linhe's establishment.
s0088.idiomatic: He was moved to recorder in the staff of the central army Prince of Linhe's establishment.

s0091.literal: Collation variant: [city] served as inspector of Yangzhou, Editorial footnote marker 2. Gu Ye and Wang Bao of Langye were both retainers; the prince greatly cherished their talent.
s0091.idiomatic: Collation variant: [city], the prince served as inspector of Yangzhou, [2] and Gu Ye and Wang Bao of Langye were both his retainers; the prince greatly prized their gifts.

s0092.literal: Ye also loved cinnabar green and was skilled at drawing and depiction; the prince raised a studio in the eastern mansion and had Ye paint the ancient worthies and Wang Bao compose encomia—men of the time called them the twin marvels.
s0092.idiomatic: Ye also loved ink and color and was skilled at drawing. The prince built a studio in the eastern mansion, had Ye paint the ancient worthies and Wang Bao write their praises—men of the time called the pair a double wonder.

s0093.literal: When Hou Jing's turmoil came, Ye was mourning his father and returned to his home commandery; he then recruited several hundred men of his native place and followed the loyal army to relieve the capital.
s0093.idiomatic: When Hou Jing's rebellion broke out, Ye was mourning his father and went home; he then recruited several hundred men of his township and marched with the loyal army to relieve the capital.

s0094.literal: Ye's frame had always been slight and frail; he was barely six chi tall, and in mourning he had wasted beyond bearing clothes—yet when he took spear and donned armor, set forth the righteousness of ruler and minister and the principle of obedience and rebellion, and spoke with defiant color, all who saw him felt emboldened.
s0094.idiomatic: Ye had always been slight of build, barely six feet, and in mourning had wasted until his robes hung loose—yet when he took spear and donned armor, spoke of the bond between ruler and minister and the line between loyalty and rebellion, and flushed with defiance as he spoke, every witness felt his spirit rise.

s0095.literal: When the capital fell, Ye fled to Kuaiji, then went on to Dongyang, and with Liu Guiyi united armies to hold the city and resist the rebels.
s0095.idiomatic: When the capital fell, Ye fled to Kuaiji, then went to Dongyang and joined Liu Guiyi in holding the city against the rebels.

s0096.literal: When Hou Jing was pacified, Grand Marshal Wang Sengbian praised him deeply and had him oversee Haiyan county.
s0096.idiomatic: After Hou Jing was crushed, grand marshal Wang Sengbian praised him deeply and made him overseer of Haiyan county.

s0097.literal: Ye from youth was known for devoted learning and utmost nature; among others he never overstepped in word or lost color in countenance—to look at his face, he seemed unable to speak—yet when he exerted his strength and acted, none could match him.
s0097.idiomatic: From youth Ye was known for devoted learning and deep feeling. Among others he never overspoke or let his face slip—to see him, you would think he could not speak at all—yet when he set his will and moved, no one could keep pace.

s0098.literal: His third younger brother Chongguo died early; Ye raised the orphaned young with deep kindness and righteousness.
s0098.idiomatic: His third younger brother Chongguo died young; Ye raised the orphaned children with deep kindness.

s0099.literal: What he compiled and wrote—the Jade Chapters in thirty juan, Topographies of the Realm in thirty juan, Diagrams of Auspicious Omens in ten juan, Genealogical Traditions of the Gu Clan in ten juan, Essentials of the Division of the Heavens in one juan, Continuation of the Records of the Hidden Realm in one juan, Tables of the Dark Signs in one juan—all circulated in his day.
s0099.idiomatic: What he wrote and compiled—the Jade Chapters in thirty juan, Topographies of the Realm in thirty juan, Diagrams of Auspicious Omens in ten juan, Genealogical Traditions of the Gu Clan in ten juan, Essentials of the Division of the Heavens in one juan, Continuation of the Records of the Hidden Realm in one juan, Tables of the Dark Signs in one juan—all circulated in his time.

s0100.literal: He also drafted Essentials of the Comprehensive History in one hundred juan and National History in Annals and Biographies in two hundred juan, but died before completion.
s0100.idiomatic: He also drafted Essentials of the Comprehensive History in one hundred juan and National History in Annals and Biographies in two hundred juan, but died before either was finished.
